lead: A sensor turns a physical stimulus into a measurable electrical change. The trick is not electrical: it is a known physical law. A force bends a beam and changes strain gauge resistance; two dissimilar metals joined at two junctions, with the junctions at different temperatures, make a small emf; light creates charge carriers. The principles group by energy domain — mechanical, thermal, electrical, magnetic, radiant, chemical — and name the measurand, the intermediate variable and the electrical output. The same law often serves two measurands; the packaging, not the equation, decides what the sensor measures. That is how a phone knows orientation and a car knows tyre pressure.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for active and passive vocabulary, and basic electricity and magnetism — charge, field, potential, Ohm's law and Faraday's law.

blocks.text: Every sensing path has five stages: stimulus → sensing element → physical law → parameter change → electrical output. The figure shows this chain. The law is the middle: it converts a non-electrical quantity into ΔR, ΔC, ΔL or Δemf. A resistance change needs a bridge or divider; a capacitance change needs an AC bridge or charge amplifier; an emf can go straight to a high-impedance amplifier. A passive sensor changes R, C or L and needs a supply; an active sensor makes its own emf (see Chapter 1.1).

Electrical quantities are the language. Charge Q is in coulombs (C). Note that C is also the usual symbol for capacitance, in farads; here the coulomb and the farad are different quantities. Electric field E = V/d is in volts per metre (V/m), with V the potential difference in volts and d the plate separation in metres. Potential energy per charge is V. For a capacitor, Q = CV, so C = Q/V, in farads (F). A parallel-plate capacitor has C = εA/d, where A is plate area in m², ε = ε₀εᵣ is permittivity in F/m, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, and εᵣ is relative permittivity. These equations are why a capacitive sensor needs a changing gap, area or dielectric.

Resistance is R = ρL/A. R is in Ω; ρ is resistivity in Ω·m; L is length in m; A is cross-section in m². Stretching a wire increases L and decreases A, so R rises. The piezoresistive effect writes this as ΔR/R = GF·ε, where GF is the gauge factor (dimensionless), ε is strain (m/m), and ΔR is the change in resistance. The effect works under steady load. A metal strain gauge has GF near 2; a semiconductor gauge is much larger but more temperature-sensitive. Typical use: a load cell weighs a truck. Construction and bridge circuits belong to Unit 2.

Piezoelectricity is different. A stress on quartz or PZT displaces charge: q = d·F, where q is charge in coulombs, d is the charge coefficient in C/N, and F is force in newtons. It gives a voltage across the crystal capacitance. It cannot hold a steady reading because the charge leaks away, so it suits vibration, impact and ultrasonic pulses. See Unit 4 for devices.

Thermal law: the Seebeck effect. Two different metals joined at two points with a temperature difference ΔT produce an emf e = S·ΔT, where S is the Seebeck coefficient in V/K. The measurand is temperature difference; the output is a small dc voltage, often µV to mV. Cold-junction compensation is needed before you can read absolute temperature; thermocouple laws are in Unit 2.

A coil has L ≈ N²µA/l, where L is inductance in henries (H), N is turns, µ is core permeability in H/m, A is core area in m², and l is magnetic path length in m. Faraday's law gives e = −N·dΦ/dt, where e is induced emf in volts, N is the number of turns, Φ is the magnetic flux through one turn in webers (Wb), and t is time in seconds; the minus sign is Lenz's law. A moving core changes reluctance and therefore L. A magnetostrictive or magneto-elastic material changes shape or permeability under stress, so a coil around it reads force. Hall effect: V_H = K_H·I·B/t, where V_H is Hall voltage in volts, K_H is the Hall coefficient (m³/C), I is current in amperes, B is flux density in tesla, and t is sheet thickness in metres. It senses magnetic field or, with a fixed magnet, position. See Unit 4.

Radiant laws: the photovoltaic effect gives an emf when light creates electron–hole pairs across a junction; the photoconductive effect lowers resistance when photons add carriers. The measurand is irradiance or wavelength; the intermediate is carrier generation; the output is emf or ΔR. A photodiode in a light meter is one use. Photodiodes and phototransistors are in Unit 4.

Chemical: a hygroscopic layer absorbs water, changing its resistance or capacitance. The measurand is relative humidity; the intermediate is water uptake; the output is ΔR or ΔC. A capacitor can sense displacement or humidity: the equation C = εA/d is the same, but one package lets pressure change d, and another lets humidity change εᵣ. Packaging decides. See Unit 5 for humidity sensors.

figure.caption: The path from stimulus to electrical output. The shaded parameter-change box is where the physical law acts; the final reading is only as reliable as that law and the packaging around it.

spec.title: One sensing path
spec.aria: A downward chain from the stimulus through the sensing element and the governing physical law to a change in an electrical parameter and finally to a readable electrical output.

examples.question: A capacitive pressure sensor has two plates of area A = 25 mm² separated by d = 0.10 mm of air (εᵣ ≈ 1, ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m). Pressure pushes the gap down by 0.01 mm. Find C before and after, the change in pF, the percentage change, and the small-signal sensitivity |dC/dd| at the start in pF/µm.
steps: Convert: A = 25 mm² = 25×10⁻⁶ m². Initial gap d₁ = 0.10 mm = 1.0×10⁻⁴ m. New gap d₂ = 0.10 − 0.01 = 0.09 mm = 9.0×10⁻⁵ m. Air gives ε = ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m.

Small-signal sensitivity at the start: |dC/dd| = ε₀A/d₁² = C₁/d₁ = 2.2135×10⁻¹² / 1.0×10⁻⁴ = 2.2135×10⁻⁸ F/m. Since 1 pF/µm = 1×10⁻⁶ F/m, this is 0.0221 pF/µm ≈ 0.022 pF/µm. The sign is negative physically: C rises as d falls.
examples.check:
eps0 = 8.854e-12
A = 25e-6
d1 = 0.10e-3
d2 = 0.09e-3
C1 = eps0 * A / d1
C2 = eps0 * A / d2
delta = C2 - C1
pct = delta / C1 * 100
sens = C1 / d1
print(round(C1 * 1e12, 2))
print(round(C2 * 1e12, 2))
print(round(delta * 1e12, 2))
print(round(pct, 1))
print(round(sens * 1e6, 3))

traps: Do not confuse piezoresistive with piezoelectric. Piezoresistive changes resistance under strain and works for steady loads; piezoelectric makes charge under stress and cannot hold a steady reading without charge leakage.

The capacitance formula is non-linear in d. A 10 % reduction in gap (d falls to 0.9 d) raises C by about 11 % (1/0.9 = 1.111), not 10 %; a 10 % increase in gap lowers C by about 9.1 %. The relation is non-linear and not symmetric.
A Seebeck emf depends on the temperature difference, not the absolute temperature. A thermocouple still needs a cold junction before it reports absolute temperature.
In V_H = K_H·I·B/t, the thickness t is in the denominator. Doubling the sheet thickness halves the Hall voltage for the same current and field.
A photovoltaic cell gives an emf; a photoconductive cell changes resistance and needs a bias supply. They are not interchangeable circuits.

quiz.q: State the piezoresistive relation and define GF and ε.
quiz.a: ΔR/R = GF·ε. GF is the gauge factor, dimensionless. ε is strain, ΔL/L, dimensionless. ΔR/R is the fractional change in resistance.

quiz.q: Why can a piezoresistive strain gauge hold a steady reading under a constant force, while a piezoelectric sensor cannot?
quiz.a: A piezoresistive gauge changes resistance as long as the strain exists, so a DC bridge can read it. A piezoelectric crystal produces charge q = d·F, but that charge leaks through the crystal and the circuit, so the output decays. It needs a changing force.

quiz.q: A parallel-plate capacitive sensor has A = 100 mm² and d = 0.20 mm of air. Find C. The gap then falls to 0.18 mm. Find the new C and the percentage change.
The same parallel-plate capacitor can be sold as a displacement sensor or a humidity sensor. What changes in each package, and why is the equation not enough to tell them apart?
quiz.a: Both use C = εA/d. In the displacement package, the measurand moves the plates and changes d. In the humidity package, a hygroscopic dielectric absorbs water and changes εᵣ. The equation is identical; the packaging and the exposed material decide which variable the outside world can change.

quiz.q: A thermocouple has Seebeck coefficient S = 40 µV/°C and sees a temperature difference ΔT = 25 °C. Find the emf.
A Hall sensor follows V_H = K_H·I·B/t. What happens to V_H if the active sheet is made thinner, with the same current and field?
quiz.a: V_H rises inversely with t. Halving t doubles V_H for the same I and B. Practical limits are resistance, self-heating and mechanical strength of the thin sheet.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same laws reappear in MEMS: a piezoresistive diaphragm in a phone barometer, a thermopile in an infrared thermometer, a capacitive humidity layer in a weather station. Automotive and medical products combine several principles on one chip and use packaging to isolate the measurand. Search next for MEMS piezoresistive pressure sensor, thin-film thermopile, and capacitive humidity sensor.
